record.original_question: Develop an algorithmic procedure that, given an ordinary differential equation with the Painleve property, decides whether the equation can be solved in terms of one of the Painleve equations or an associated Painleve sigma-equation.

evidence.quote: Develop algorithmic procedures for the Painleve equivalence problem: given an equation with the Painleve property, how do we know if the equation can be solved in terms of a Painleve equation (or a Painleve sigma-equation)?
Open Problem 2.9. Given an ordinary differential equation with the Painleve property, how do we know whether it can be solved in terms of a Painleve transcendent?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An ordinary differential equation is said to have the Painlevé property if every movable singularity of every solution (i.e., a singularity whose location depends on the initial conditions) is a pole. The six Painlevé equations P_I, ..., P_VI are the canonical second-order ODEs with the Painlevé property whose general solutions define new transcendental functions (the Painlevé transcendents); to each Painlevé equation P_J there is also an associated Hamiltonian "sigma-equation" (the Painlevé sigma-equation) satisfied by an auxiliary Hamiltonian function.

Problem. Devise an algorithmic procedure (taking as input an ordinary differential equation that is known to have the Painlevé property) which decides, in finitely many effective steps, whether the given equation can be solved in closed form in terms of one of the Painlevé equations P_I,...,P_VI or one of the associated Painlevé sigma-equations, and, when it can, produces an explicit transformation reducing the given equation to that Painlevé (or sigma-) equation.
artifact.status_search_result: The Painlevé equivalence problem remains an active area of research with no fully general algorithm known. Recent work using algebro-geometric methods (Okamoto's spaces of initial conditions, iterative blow-up regularisation) has produced essentially algorithmic step-by-step identification procedures that work for specific classes of systems (e.g., Bureau–Guillot systems, certain constrained 3D systems, identifications with Painlevé VI), so the problem is partially solved in those settings but a complete general algorithm has not been established.

status_evidence.title: Quadratic Bureau-Guillot systems with the first and second Painlevé transcendents in the coefficients. Part I
status_evidence.snippet: explains birational equivalence using Okamoto's spaces of initial conditions and iterative polynomial regularisation methods, solving the Painlevé equivalence problem for Bureau-Guillot systems
status_evidence.claim: Recent algebro-geometric algorithmic procedures solve the Painlevé equivalence problem for specific system classes.

status_evidence.title: The Painlevé equivalence problem for a constrained 3D system
status_evidence.snippet: Painlevé identification algorithm used to relate a constrained 3D system to the Painlevé VI equation
status_evidence.claim: Algorithmic identification with specific Painlevé equations has been carried out in particular cases.

status_evidence.title: Painlevé transcendents - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The six Painlevé equations define new transcendental functions; classifying ODEs with the Painlevé property up to equivalence with these is an ongoing research problem.
status_evidence.claim: No fully general algorithm is known for the Painlevé equivalence problem.
